metadata.label: MATISSE reconstruction
metadata.coverage: One image of the photosphere reconstructed with the public SQUEEZE code from 780 squared visibilities and 520 closure phases measured by VLT/MATISSE on 8 and 19 February 2020 in the 3.94-4.00 micrometre pseudo-continuum, convolved to the 4 milliarcsecond interferometric beam and cast onto a sphere of the published radius. The camera is computed: the rotation pole lies in the plane of the sky at the ALMA position angle, the display meridian is the sub-Earth point at the epoch, and the pixel scale is the reconstruction's. Nothing finer than the beam is shown: the raw reconstruction carries sub-beam texture the visibilities never constrained. The bright and dark patches are not confirmed as surface features: a spotless disc reconstructed from the same coverage, at sizes within 2 percent of the star's, leaves patches up to as strong. Negating every closure phase fits the data equally well, so which side of the star is brighter is weakly constrained. The colours are a legend for reconstructed relative intensity in one infrared band, the paper's heat scale from dark red to white, not colour or temperature. The far hemisphere is unobserved.

transfer.interpretation: Trial acceptance bounds, not estimates of source accuracy. A footprint is the pixel's range times its angular size, 19.6 million kilometres at the disc centre from 168 parsecs, so a contributor lies within two of those of the closest sphere point; the one-metre visibility tolerance is numerically zero on a body this size, and the sphere is convex, so no point occludes another.

metadata.label: MATISSE December 2018
metadata.coverage: One image of the photosphere reconstructed with the public SQUEEZE code from 3240 squared visibilities and 2160 closure phases measured by VLT/MATISSE on eight nights from 3 to 15 December 2018 in the 3.94-4.00 micrometre pseudo-continuum, with the February 2020 recipe unchanged, convolved to the 3 milliarcsecond beam of this epoch's longest baseline and cast onto a sphere of the published radius. The camera is computed as for February 2020. The reconstruction does not reach the check: it fits the closure phases at reduced chi-squared 3.03 against a limit of 3, and a spotless disc from the same coverage leaves patches as strong (ratio 1.04, limit 2). The bright and dark patches are therefore not confirmed as surface features. The colours are a legend for reconstructed relative intensity in one infrared band, the paper's heat scale, not colour or temperature. The far hemisphere is unobserved.

metadata.label: MATISSE December 2020
metadata.coverage: One image of the photosphere reconstructed with the public SQUEEZE code from 1248 squared visibilities and 832 closure phases measured by VLT/MATISSE on three nights on 14, 18 and 27 December 2020 in the 3.94-4.00 micrometre pseudo-continuum, with the February 2020 recipe unchanged, convolved to the 3.1 milliarcsecond beam of this epoch's longest baseline and cast onto a sphere of the published radius. The camera is computed as for February 2020. The reconstruction fits its data (reduced chi-squared 0.53 and 1.77), but a spotless disc from the same coverage leaves patches as strong (ratio 0.87, limit 2), and the two halves of the data agree only at 0.45 (limit 0.5). The bright and dark patches are therefore not confirmed as surface features. The colours are a legend for reconstructed relative intensity in one infrared band, the paper's heat scale, not colour or temperature. The far hemisphere is unobserved.

controls.label: MATISSE reconstruction
controls.notes: An image of the photosphere reconstructed by the public SQUEEZE code from public VLT/MATISSE visibilities and closure phases of 8 and 19 February 2020, in the 3.94-4.00 micrometre continuum, convolved to the 4 milliarcsecond interferometric beam and cast onto a sphere of the published radius, so nothing finer than the beam is shown. Its bright and dark patches are not confirmed as surface features: a spotless disc reconstructed from the same coverage, at sizes within 2 percent of the star's, leaves patches up to as strong. Negating every closure phase fits equally well, so which limb is brighter is weakly constrained. The colours are a legend for reconstructed relative intensity in one infrared band, the paper's heat scale: not colour, temperature or albedo. A fifth of the reconstruction's flux lies outside the disc, and it is drawn here in three dimensions rather than as a flat plate behind the sphere: the envelope that best projects to its measured radial profile, which falls as r to the minus eight. The ring within one beam of the limb is left out, because there the light is the star's own edge smeared by the 4 milliarcsecond beam rather than anything resolved; that is about half of the off-limb flux. What is drawn is the extended emission the visibilities require. The far hemisphere and the poles were not observed.

legend.title: Relative intensity at 4 µm
legend.meta: fraction of the brightest point · 1st–99.5th percentile stretch

controls.label: Polarised dust · December 2024
controls.notes: The photosphere as the MATISSE reconstruction shows it, with the dust around it: the degree of linear polarisation VLT/SPHERE-ZIMPOL measured in the V band on 3 December 2024, released by ESO as Phase 3 collection BETELGEUSE-B beside Montargès et al. (2026). The patches one to about 4.5 stellar radii out are starlight scattered by dust. This is their own Fig. B.1 given depth: the same inferno colour map on the same zero-to-0.10 scale, carried as four emission channels so a line of sight emits the bar colour of its own measured degree. The colours are a legend for a ratio, not the colour of the dust. The instrumental polarisation measured beyond eight radii is subtracted, so the empty sky is darker here than in the printed figure. The map is a sky-plane image with no third axis, so the depth is inferred rather than pushed back from the sky: the azimuthally averaged radial profile is fitted with simple envelopes around the star, and the one that projects to it is a spherical shell of 3.5 stellar radii and gaussian thickness 1.2, which beats both a steady outflow and the constant depth an extrusion assumes. Each patch is placed on that shell, in front of the star and behind it, because nothing in one image says which. That shape is an inference from the profile, not a measurement.

legend.title: Degree of linear polarisation
legend.meta: V band, 3 December 2024 · the paper's own inferno scale

controls.label: Great Dimming clump · December 2019
controls.notes: The same photosphere, with the dust clump Montargès et al. (2021) fitted to the Great Dimming, drawn from the numbers they published for December 2019: a sphere of uniform density south and slightly west of the star and between it and us. Its extinction is scaled so the line of sight through its centre dims the star ten times, as they report for the southern hemisphere, and the light it scatters back is drawn faintly over that. A model fitted to images, not an image.

controls.label: SiO envelope · August 2023
controls.notes: The same photosphere, with the silicon monoxide ALMA saw around it in August 2023. This is the only dataset here placed in depth by its own measured velocities rather than by a shape fitted to a picture. Everything is measured from the star itself, which the same observation's continuum places a tenth of an arcsecond, nearly five stellar radii, from where ALMA pointed. In front of the star the molecule absorbs its light, some of it leaving the star and some falling back; around it, the molecule glows in a lopsided ring between two and four stellar radii out, heaviest to the east-south-east. Each channel of the line cube is placed along the line of sight on a spherical outflow at the speed of the fastest gas absorbing in front of the star, about twenty-two kilometres a second, which is the usual first reading of an expanding stellar envelope. Gas that is falling back is placed as if it were flowing out, so the depths are a model. Silicon monoxide is what silicate dust condenses from, so this is the material of the other datasets caught before it became dust. The colours are a false-colour ramp for line brightness, not colour or temperature.

legend.title: SiO line brightness, integrated
legend.meta: fraction of the peak · ALMA band 6, 217.105 GHz · viridis, false colour

controls.label: Color
controls.qualification: Colour from a measured spectrum of the star (VLT/X-shooter). The disc is unresolved, and no darkening toward the edge is measured.
controls.notes: The colour of Betelgeuse's VLT/X-shooter spectrum. It was taken on 12 October 2009, before the Great Dimming, and is not corrected for light lost at the slit, which can tilt the colour. No resolved image of the surface is cast here.
